analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers once again deny coverage to children with pre-existing conditions.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, died in committee without a vote, leaving the new ban on denying sick children coverage in place.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the part of the new health care law that says health insurers cannot refuse to cover children under 19, or charge them more, because they are already sick. That ban took effect when the Affordable Care Act was signed. The bill went nowhere: one member introduced it, no one else signed on, and the committee it was sent to never acted before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Health insurers, who would regain the ability to refuse coverage, set higher prices, or exclude a child's known condition for enrollees under 19. Insurers had raised this objection most strongly in the small 'child-only' insurance market, where families buy policies directly rather than through an employer.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Affordable Care Act rule that bars group plans and insurers from imposing pre-existing condition exclusions on enrollees under 19, effective as of the bill's enactment.
Without that rule, insurers could again use medical underwriting for children: refusing to sell a policy to a sick child, charging more, or writing the child's known illness out of the policy.

analysis.who_pays: Families with children who have existing health problems. These are the children most likely to need expensive care, so they are exactly who an insurer has the strongest business reason to turn away or price out of coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Families of children with health conditions

drawbacks.text: The protection the bill repeals is narrow: it covers only enrollees under 19, and the same Affordable Care Act section leaves all other anti-discrimination rules untouched, so even if enacted it would change coverage for one age group only.

A good-faith objection insurers and some economists raise against banning pre-existing condition exclusions without a broader risk pool: if insurers must accept any sick child at standard rates, healthy families have an incentive to wait until a child gets sick to buy coverage, which can push premiums up for everyone in the small child-only market.
Repealing the rule takes effect the day of enactment, which would leave children who had just gained guaranteed coverage with no transition period and no substitute protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go entirely to insurers, in the form of the right to turn away or surcharge the costliest young customers. The cost falls on a small, high-need group: children who already have health problems and their families, for whom insurance is hardest to get and most needed. There is no offsetting benefit in the bill for ordinary people.

outcome.mechanism: One representative introduced it and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which never acted on it before that Congress ended, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gary Ackerman introduced the bill in the House on November 29, 2010.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill never received a vote in committee or on the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sick children and their families, who kept the new protection, and no industry gained anything, since the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Gary Ackerman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act's ban on pre-existing condition exclusions for children under 19.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; took no action
against.what_they_did: Never voted the bill out of committee or scheduled any action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: A single House Democrat introduced the bill, no one cosponsored it, and it never came to a vote, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would restore their ability to refuse coverage, charge more, or exclude a child's known illness for enrollees under 19. Those children are the customers insurers have the strongest financial reason to avoid, so the industry's gain here comes directly at the expense of the families the protections cover.
